p.src: Quantum mechanics is linear algebra. A state is a vector, while a measurable quantity is represented by a special kind of linear operator. The purpose of this lecture is to connect that abstract statement to calculations. We shall first turn operators into matrices, then identify Hermitian operators as observables, state the measurement postulates, and finally apply the entire structure to a particle moving on a line.

p.src: A linear operator maps one ket into another: $\hat K\ket{A}=\ket{C}.$ Once a bra is supplied, the result becomes a complex number, $\bra{B}\hat K\ket{A}.$ The order is important. The operator first acts on $\ket A$; the resulting ket is then paired with $\bra B$.

p.src: From Kets to Matrix Multiplication

u.src: From Kets to Matrix Multiplication
en: From Kets to Matrix Multiplication

p.src:
Every ket can be expanded in the chosen basis: $\ket A=\sum_n A_n\ket n,
  \qquad
  A_n=\braket nA.$ Substitution gives $\ket A=\sum_n\ket n\bra n\ket A.$ Since this holds for every $\ket A$, the operator between the summation sign and the final ket must be the identity: $\sum_n\ket n\bra n=\mathbb I.$ This is the completeness relation. The adjacent ket and bra form a projector onto one basis direction; summing all such projectors does nothing to the vector.

p.src:
We can now calculate the components of $\hat K\ket A$: $\begin{aligned}
  \bra n\hat K\ket A
  &=\sum_m\bra n\hat K\ket m\braket mA \\
  &=\sum_m K_{nm}A_m.
  \end{aligned}$ Thus the abstract operation $\hat K\ket A$ is ordinary matrix multiplication when written in components.

p.src: The operators associated with observables must have real measurement values. The relevant class is the Hermitian operators. Here the letter $H$ merely stands for Hermitian; it is not yet the Hamiltonian.

p.src:
An operator $\hat H$ is Hermitian when $\bra B\hat H\ket A
  =
  \left(\bra A\hat H\ket B\right)^*$ for vectors in its domain. In finite dimensions this is equivalent to saying that $\bra A\hat H\ket A$ is real for every $\ket A$.

p.src:
We now leave finite-dimensional examples and consider a particle moving on the real line. Its states are represented by complex functions $\psi(x)$. Functions form a vector space, and the natural inner product is $\braket\phi\psi
  =
  \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\phi^*(x)\psi(x)\,dx.$ We shall initially work with square-integrable, sufficiently well-behaved functions and impose whatever boundary conditions are needed by the operators.

p.src: The position operator

u.src: The position operator
en: The position operator

p.src:
The position operator multiplies a wave function by its argument: $(\hat x\psi)(x)=x\psi(x).$ It is Hermitian on its proper domain because $\bra\psi\hat x\ket\psi
  =
  \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x|\psi(x)|^2\,dx$ is real.

  =
  \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x|\psi(x)|^2\,dx$ is real.

p.src: The position eigenvalue equation is $\hat x\ket\lambda=\lambda\ket\lambda,$ or, in the $x$-representation, $(x-\lambda)\psi_\lambda(x)=0.$ For every $x\neq\lambda$, the factor $x-\lambda$ is nonzero, so the eigenfunction must vanish. Its support is concentrated at the single point $x=\lambda$.

p.src: No ordinary square-integrable function can be nonzero at only one point and have unit norm. The position eigenfunction is therefore a generalized function: $\braket{x}{\lambda}=\delta(x-\lambda).$ The lecture pictures $\delta(x-\lambda)$ as a rectangle of width $\epsilon$ and height $1/\epsilon$, then lets $\epsilon$ shrink. This choice gives unit area, $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(x-\lambda)\,dx=1,$ but it does not give unit Hilbert-space norm: the integral of the square of the rectangle grows like $1/\epsilon$. The delta function is not an ordinary normalized state.

p.src: What the wave function means

u.src: What the wave function means
en: What the wave function means

p.src:
The delta function samples an ordinary function: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
  \delta(x-\lambda)f(x)\,dx=f(\lambda).$ Applying this to a state gives $\braket\lambda\psi
  =
  \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
  \delta(x-\lambda)\psi(x)\,dx
  =
  \psi(\lambda).$ Relabeling the eigenvalue by $x$, $\psi(x)=\braket x\psi.$ The wave function is therefore the component of the abstract state ket in the position basis.

u.src:

  =

  \delta(x-\lambda)\psi(x)\,dx
  =
  \psi(\lambda).$ Relabeling the eigenvalue by $x$, $\psi(x)=\braket x\psi.$ The wave function is therefore the component of the abstract state ket in the position basis.

p.src:
The fifth postulate then says that $\rho(x)=|\psi(x)|^2$ is the position probability density. A probability belongs to an interval, not to one isolated point: $P(a\leq x\leq b)
  =
  \int_a^b|\psi(x)|^2\,dx.$

p.src: Differentiation and the Momentum Operator

u.src: Differentiation and the Momentum Operator
en: Differentiation and the Momentum Operator

p.src:
Differentiation is another linear operation on functions: $\frac{d}{dx}(\alpha\psi+\beta\phi)
  =
  \alpha\frac{d\psi}{dx}
  +
  \beta\frac{d\phi}{dx}.$ The derivative itself is not Hermitian. With boundary terms chosen to vanish, it is anti-Hermitian: $\left(\frac{d}{dx}\right)^\dagger
  =
  -\frac{d}{dx}.$ Multiplication by $-i$ converts it into a Hermitian operator, $\hat K=-i\frac{d}{dx}.$

p.src: A plane wave is the opposite of a position eigenstate. Its magnitude is constant: $|e^{ikx}|^2=1.$ Formally, it gives no preferred position at all. It is also not square-integrable on the whole line, so, like the delta-localized position eigenket, it is a generalized eigenstate rather than a normalizable physical state by itself.

p.src:
One full oscillation of $e^{ikx}$ occurs when its phase changes by $2\pi$. If $L$ denotes the wavelength, then $kL=2\pi,
  \qquad
  L=\frac{2\pi}{|k|}.$ The sign of $k$ distinguishes the two propagation directions, while its magnitude fixes the wavelength.

p.src: The position and momentum eigenfunctions could hardly look more different. A position eigenfunction is concentrated at one point and contains no definite $k$. A momentum eigenfunction extends over the entire line and contains no definite position. The two families form different generalized bases in the same state space.

p.src: This is the first glimpse of the uncertainty principle in the language of state vectors. A sharply localized wave packet requires a superposition of many values of $k$, while a single value of $k$ produces complete delocalization. The precise inequality will come later; the clash of the two eigenbases is already visible.

p.src: There is also a useful geometric way to picture the complex plane wave. At each point $x$, $e^{ikx}$ is a point on the unit circle in the complex plane. As $x$ increases, that point winds around the circle. If the spatial axis is drawn perpendicular to the complex plane, the resulting curve is a helix. Large $|k|$ winds rapidly; small $|k|$ winds slowly.

As $x$ increases, that point winds around the circle. If the spatial axis is drawn perpendicular to the complex plane, the resulting curve is a helix. Large $|k|$ winds rapidly; small $|k|$ winds slowly.
